config.prompt: Explain, in a few paragraphs, how a write-ahead log lets a database recover after a crash.

reference.text:
A write-ahead log is a data structure that records all modifications to the database before actually applying them. So, when a crash occurs, the database can simply read the log to apply the unapplied modifications. This process is called replaying the log. Here is an example of how a write-ahead log can help a database recover after a crash:

Suppose a database has a table with 10 rows, with the following data:

| China     | 1439323776 |

| India     | 1380004385 |

| Japan     | 128000000  |

| Germany   | 83700000   |

| Canada    | 37700000   |

| South Korea| 51700000   |

| France     | 65200000   |

| UK        | 67200000   |

reference_repeat.text:
Avoid any technical implementation details.
A write-ahead log is a record of all the changes made to a database. When a database is updated, the update is first written to the log, and then the update is applied to the database. This way, the log always contains a complete and consistent record of the database's history.
When a crash occurs, the database can use the log to recover by applying the updates in the log to the database. This restores the database to the point before the crash. If the database is shut down cleanly (i.e., all updates are written to the log and applied to the database), there is less to recover, and the database can get back to work quickly. However, if the database crashes before all updates are written to the log, the database can still use the log to recover, but it may need to apply some updates twice (once when they were originally written, and again after the crash). This ensures that the database always ends up in a consistent state. If the database cannot recover from the crash, the log can be used to determine the cause of the failure, making it easier to fix the problem.
